title: Eleven Years of It
logline: The finest carved stone of its century in this country is a flight of about thirty-five steps on the flank of a rock, cut as the approach to a relic house for a capital that a Pali chronicle allows something like eleven years, and the film looks at one riser of it in flat midday light for as long as it takes to stop admiring the work.
human_question: If all that survives of a decade of somebody's hardest work is the work itself, what does the work actually tell me about the wanting behind it?

place.what_kind_of_place: A granite mass rising abruptly out of flat dry-zone country, with the earth ramparts and moats of a fortified town still legible at its southern foot, and on its southern flank three flights of stone stair climbing to a carved doorway and the outline of a small building — not to the top. The last of those flights carries the most elaborate figure carving of its century on the island: risers cut with a female dancer between two male drummers, panel after panel, each figure about the width of a hand; balustrades ending in makaras; crouching dwarfs; and at the bottom two lions larger than any other lion sculpture surviving from the old kingdoms. The rock was a Buddhist monastery for centuries before it was ever a royal city, and became one again afterwards: at the top there is a ruined brick stupa, a bodhi-tree enclosure and a pond, and at the foot caves with images, later paintings and one early Brahmi inscription. It is a ticketed archaeological site with a small museum, and on most days it is close to empty.
place.why_it_is_worth_watching: Two things, and neither of them is a view. First the carving, which does not need help: granite figures a few inches high, cut with a confidence that reads at macro distance, repeated along a flight so that the camera can hold one panel and know there are more of them either side of the frame. Second the geometry of the thing, which is faintly absurd and completely visible — a monumental ceremonial stair, narrow enough in places that a person has to go up it sideways, set at a steep angle on the side of a rock, arriving at a doorway with sky behind it and a platform beyond that is now an outline on the ground. Filmed square-on at midday with a long lens, the flight stops looking like a climb and starts looking like what it is: a worked surface, standing at an angle, with nothing on the other side of it.
place.what_moves_or_changes: Almost nothing, and that is the treatment rather than a shortcoming. The stair faces roughly south and holds the sun for most of the day, so the light does not swing dramatically across the relief; a passing cloud changes the exposure by a stop and changes nothing else. What changes across the film is only the camera's distance — the whole rock, then the flight, then one panel, then one riser — and the one number the voice keeps returning to. Heat shimmer works at the base in the dry months. Monkeys cross. A visitor or two goes up and comes back down. The rock itself is the only thing in the frame with a history and it does not do anything.
place.when_it_looks_best: The dry months, and then the middle of the day — roughly ten to two, with the sun high and the south-facing flight lit flat and frontally. This is the hour most films avoid and it is the hour this one needs: raking low light would turn the carving into chiaroscuro and make a spectacle of the labour, which is the exact reading the film exists to refuse. A flat overcast is equally good and arguably better. There is no dawn in this film, no dusk and no night.

two_layers.without_the_philosophy: A film that never leaves the ground and never climbs anything. It is built out of locked frames at decreasing distance: a rock standing alone in flat country at midday, then a stair on its side, then the figures on the stair, then one step, held. There is no aircraft, no golden hour, no crowd and no arrival. It resolves on its own terms, because the last frame is the first frame again, unchanged, and in between the viewer has been brought close enough to a piece of thirteenth-century granite to see the tool marks in it. Someone who never hears a word of the narration gets a complete piece about a surface, a duration, and how good somebody once was with a chisel.
two_layers.with_the_philosophy: The same frames become the sources' flattest and least comfortable claim: that energy has no moral colour of its own. The books list six working parts of any purposeful moment and insist none of them is good or bad in itself, and their picture for effort is a boat set on water already running downhill — it needs nothing from anybody, and doing good is the same load carried up a hill, where you have to put the effort in yourself. So the film spends its whole length looking at extraordinary effort in granite and declines, out loud, to call it a virtue. The second concept supplies the sorting the site cannot deliver: the sources sort wanting by whether it came glowing or came flat, whether it arrived with a story that excused it, and whether it rose on its own or had to be pushed — and they rank the flat above the glad. A carved step reports none of the three. The voice says so, and that refusal is the film.

sequence.on_screen: Flat high daylight, no cloud. One locked frame from the level of the plain, a long way back: a granite mass standing straight out of flat dry country, the pale line of the stair on its near flank, ramparts low in the foreground. Nothing in the frame moves except heat shimmer at the base. Held far longer than is comfortable.
sequence.voice: A Pali chronicle says of the king who ruled from this rock that he did good while he dwelt here, and that after carrying on the government for eleven years he entered heaven. Eleven years. Hold that number, because everything this film is going to look at was cut for a royal city that stood for somewhere inside it, and nobody can tell you how much of it.

sequence.on_screen: Tripod unmoved, still midday. A long lens from directly in front of the ornamental flight, far enough back that the focal length flattens it: the stair stops reading as a climb and reads as a wall of steps standing at an angle. No pan, no rack focus, no move at all.
sequence.voice: The compendiums this film is about list six things that come and go in a mind. Aiming at something. Going over it. Settling on it. Pushing on. The lift you feel. And the wanting to do it. Then they are careful to say that not one of the six is good or bad by itself. Each of them takes the colour of whatever mind it happens to turn up in. The same six built this. The same six would have taken it apart.

sequence.on_screen: Closer, still locked off. A balustrade end in flat frontal light, the makara whole in frame; then a macro frame on the granite beside it — tool marks, pits, lichen. Nothing is chalked, wetted, brushed, raked or lit. Available light only.
sequence.voice: For the first of the six, the aiming, their picture is a second man lifting onto your shoulder a load you could never have got up there alone, and a hawk beating its wings hard to leave the ground. For the second, the going-over, it is that same hawk high up, crossing without beating them, and it is also a man holding a metal pot firmly in one hand while the other hand rubs it slowly, over and over. That second picture is somebody's whole afternoon here. And the books warn that the two are not one after the other. They happen in the same instant.

sequence.on_screen: One figure filling the frame: a drummer, granite, a hand's width across, shot square-on from a tripod set at the height of the step. The lens holds while a cloud crosses and the exposure moves by about a stop and nothing else changes.
sequence.voice: Effort, in these books, is the thing that will not turn back until what was begun is finished. They are specific that they mean a mental thing and not strength in the arms, which they treat as a separate item and set aside. This figure is a few inches high. There are more of them along the flight, and no two of them are doing the same thing.

sequence.on_screen: The payoff, and the only frame the film is built to get: one riser of the top flight, level, square, locked off — a female dancer between two male drummers, each figure about the width of a hand, granite, flat overhead light. Held for a long time, with no move, no cut and nothing added to the stone.
sequence.voice: It would be very easy to look at this and conclude that effort is a good thing. The books refuse. They say that in a mind already sloping the wrong way, effort runs like a boat set on water that is already flowing downhill: it gets there needing nothing from anybody. Doing good is the same load carried up a hill, and there you have to put the effort in yourself. It is the slope that settles where it goes, not the pushing. This step tells you somebody pushed. It does not tell you which way the ground was tilted.

sequence.on_screen: The porch above the flight, from below and level: a stone opening with plain sky behind it, empty. Then the same opening at a longer lens, so the emptiness is the whole frame. The camera does not go through and never turns round to look out.
sequence.voice: Two pierced stone panels came out of these porches, cut through with rings of small figures, and they are in museums now, one of them a long drive from here. The books have a second list, and it sorts wanting three ways: whether it came glowing or came flat, whether it arrived with a story that excused it, and whether it rose on its own or had to be pushed, including the pushing a person does to their own hesitating mind. Against expectation, they rank the flat above the glad, and the unpushed above the pushed. Look at the hole where the panel was and tell me which of the three you can see.

sequence.on_screen: The threshold stone at the head of the flight, filmed straight down from standing height: granite worn smooth in two places and sharp everywhere else. Then a wide static frame of the platform beyond it, which is an outline on the ground and some courses of brick.
sequence.voice: This was the way up to a relic house. The chronicle says a famine came; that five brother kings on the mainland sent a general called Ariyacakkavatti; that he entered the stronghold, took the Tooth Relic and the treasures, and handed the relic to King Kulasekhara. It says the next king saw no way to get it back but friendly talk, went there himself, talked with him daily, received it from the king's own hand, and placed it in a different city. That is the whole of it. The list I just read you sorts minds, and there is not a mind anywhere in that paragraph that I am able to put on it.

sequence.on_screen: The opening frame again: same position, same lens, same hour, same light. The rock, the plain, the heat at the base. Nothing has changed and nothing is added. The film ends on it without a move.
sequence.voice: One of the six is the wanting to do a thing, and the books are insistent that it is not the same item as the sticking that will not let go — that has its own names in the lists. Trained, they say, the wanting turns and works against the sticking. They never once say it does that by itself. This surface is still here and those eleven years are over, and neither of those two facts is a verdict on anybody.

concept_merge.why_together: Read fresh, these two digests are a mechanism and the anatomy the mechanism is deliberately kept out of. C021 is the sources' working drawing of any purposeful moment: six factors that are present in some minds and absent in others, that occur in wholesome and unwholesome minds alike, and that are reckoned wholesome, unwholesome or neither according to the mind they join [C021-P:L25] [C021-M:L29]. Their examples are manual: a second man raising onto your shoulder a burden you cannot lift alone, and a hawk beating its way up [C021-P:L33]; that hawk gliding, and a man gripping a metal vessel firmly in one hand while the other slowly rubs it [C021-P:L41]; effort as what does not turn back until the thing begun is finished, mental and not muscular [C021-M:L19]; and effort in a mind already inclined to harm running like a boat on water already flowing downhill, against the good deed that is a load carried uphill and has to be pushed [C021-P:L53]. C006 is the other book: the anatomy of wanting that sticks, set by three dials — glad on a pleasing object [C006-P:L25] or flat on a neutral one [C006-P:L74]; with or without a view that denies consequences or excuses the act [C006-P:L33]; and either arising sharply of its own nature [C006-P:L44] or needing to be urged, by somebody else or by the person talking their own hesitating mind round [C006-M:L5]. The Margaya then ranks them, and the ranking is the reason this pairing works: view-backed above view-free, unprompted above prompted, and — against expectation — flat above glad [C006-M:L19]. A carved stair is the one subject on which both can be set down honestly, because the site supplies an enormous quantity of the first book's material and not one item of the second's. The effort is in the granite, measurable, still there after seven hundred years. Which of C006's three dials was set which way in whoever ordered it, paid for it or cut it is not recoverable from stone, and the film says so out loud instead of guessing.
concept_merge.what_it_reveals: That the interesting question about a masterpiece is not how much work went into it. C021 alone would be a lecture with six headings. C006 alone, pointed at a thirteenth-century king and his stonemasons, would be an accusation dressed as doctrine, and in a group whose subject is the greed-rooted minds that is the specific failure to avoid. Put together on one flight of steps they produce something neither could: the sources' flattest claim, standing in front of the best evidence against it. Here is effort that nobody disputes — the finest figure carving of its century on the island — and here are the same books saying effort is not a merit, that it runs downhill as readily as up, and that the wanting which drove it is not even the same item as the wanting that clings. The pairing also closes both exits the digests name by hand. It cannot become 'follow your passion', because C021 says the same wish inside a greed-rooted mind simply strengthens the greed. And it cannot become 'hard work is virtuous', because C021 gives effort a downstream boat for a picture and no colour of its own.

concept_links.why: The digest's own similes are the physical facts of this site rather than analogies laid over it. Initial application is pictured as another man raising onto your shoulder a load you could not lift alone, and as a hawk beating its wings hard to climb [C021-P:L33]; sustained application is the same hawk crossing the sky without beating, and a man gripping a metal vessel firmly in one hand while the other rubs it slowly over and over [C021-P:L41] — which is not a figure of speech for a carver holding a chisel against granite, it is a description of the job. Effort is what does not turn back until the thing begun is finished, and the Margaya is explicit that the mental factor is meant and that bodily strength is a different item altogether [C021-M:L19], which is why this film can stand on a carved surface without making it a film about labour. The load-bearing line is the group's own: desire-to-act is the wish to take up the object and not the power that makes one stick to it, and that adhesion is given its own separate names [C021-P:L69], which the Margaya repeats as a wanting with none of greed's adhesion in it [C021-M:L27]; developed, it becomes a predominant factor and a base of success, and it then works against craving rather than for it [C021-P:L75]. Five of the digest's limits are written into the film rather than parked in the risks. First, the six factors have no colour of their own and take the colour of the mind they join [C021-P:L25], which beat 2 says out loud so that nobody who made this is called good for having tried hard. Second — and this is the film's spine — effort is not a virtue: in a mind already inclined to harm it runs like a boat set on water already flowing downhill, while the good deed is the same load carried uphill and has to be pushed [C021-P:L53]. That is beat 5, spoken over the single most beautiful frame in the film, which is the only place it does any work. Third, the Margaya's warning that the bell simile makes the first two factors look consecutive when they arise in one instant [C021-M:L11] is spoken in beat 3, because a stair is exactly the location that invites a start-then-continue reading. Fourth, the account of rapture lifting and shaking the body through the air element is traditional physiology [C021-P:L61] [C021-P:L63], so nothing in this film — no carved dancer, no drummer, no visitor, no monk — is described in narration as rapture, gladness or absorption, and the carved figures are filmed as carving and never as evidence of a state. Fifth, the decision factor settles firmly on an object whether the settling is right or wrong and is frequently wrong [C021-P:L45], and the Margaya calls it hard to discern at all [C021-M:L15], which is a standing reason the film does not read certainty, conviction or resolve into anybody's building programme. Two further digest lines are respected by omission: the claim that the sound of initial application can be heard by the divine ear is flagged in the digest's own uncertainties, and the thirteen ethically variable factors [C021-M:L31] are a classification the film has no use for. The seventh beat's sentence about the sorting list not reaching anybody is the digest's neutrality applied to history rather than to a person in frame.

Kept, narrowed to the one thing the digest genuinely supplies here, and used with its own category declined out loud. What C006 offers a film about a stair is a sorting scheme and a ranking, both of which turn out to be unanswerable from stone. The three dials are the digest's own reading: gladness arising on a pleasing object [C006-P:L25] against flat feeling on a neutral one [C006-P:L74]; with or without a view that denies consequences or excuses the act [C006-P:L33]; and arising sharply of its own nature [C006-P:L44] against being urged, by another person or by oneself talking a hesitating mind round [C006-M:L5]. Then the Margaya's ranking, which is what makes the scheme worth filming: courses of action outweigh ordinary attachment, view-backed outweighs view-free, unprompted outweighs prompted, and neutral outweighs joyful [C006-M:L19]. Beats 6 and 7 name the scheme, apply it to nothing, and say that a carved riser reports none of the three settings. Four of the digest's guards bear directly and are built in. The wrong-view dial is named as a category and applied to no one: the digest forbids mapping wrong view onto any community's faith, and the views in question there are denials of consequence and self-serving excuses [C006-P:L33], not anybody's religion, so no king, minister, mason or monk in this record is placed on it. 'Calm means good' is refused, because the Margaya ranks flat, unexcited wanting stronger than glad wanting [C006-M:L19] and the digest's uncertainties record that the extract gives no commentarial basis for that ranking — so the film reports it as the books' own ranking and as unsettled, and never uses the stillness of the site as evidence of anything. Prompting does not absolve: prompted wanting is ranked weaker without being excused [C006-M:L19], and the sluggishness that attaches to prompted unwholesome minds [C006-P:L62] is a fact about minds and not about a building programme, so the film never suggests that anyone urged on by a court was less the author of what they did. And the conditions the Pradeepika lists as favouring one variant over another — the kind of rebirth-linking, temperament, health, patience, habit, company, suitable weather and food [C006-P:L46–L52] — describe tendencies rather than fate, do not map onto modern genetics, and are conditions of a mind rather than of a kingdom, so nothing here reads the fall of a capital as a consequence of anybody's character. The digest's most human passage, the person who fully believes in consequences and cannot master the wanting anyway, largely through long habit [C006-P:L66], is deliberately not used: it is the one line in either digest that would let this film characterise a named historical person, and it is left where it is.

what_the_viewer_could_understand: That admiring how hard somebody worked tells you nothing about the wanting behind it, and that this is not cynicism but what the books actually say: the same drive runs downhill as easily as up, and where it goes is settled by the slope and not by the pushing. The proof needs no belief and is in one frame — a few inches of granite that took real skill and real time, and that cannot tell you a single thing about the mind that ordered it.
what_must_be_real: The carving as it stands, in the light that is actually on it. Nothing is chalked, wetted, oiled, brushed, powdered, raked with a lamp or lit from the side, and no frame is graded to lift the relief; if a panel does not read in available light it is not in the film. Nothing is reconstructed, composited or restored digitally, and where a step, a balustrade or a porch has been re-set or repaired by conservators the film either says so or does not use the frame — presenting restored stonework as thirteenth-century carving would be the one dishonesty this subject cannot survive. The film uses no aircraft at all, so nothing on the site is overflown. The stair is narrow and steep and is the only way up to the doorway: no frame is set up that blocks it, and a shot that requires a visitor to wait is not taken. Visitors, monks and site staff appear only incidentally, wide or from behind, and no identifiable person is characterised in narration or framing as devout, driven, acquisitive or anything else — the group's whole subject is the greed-rooted minds and no face in this film carries any of it. There is a living temple with a shrine and later paintings at the foot of the rock: no worship is filmed, interrupted or lit, and the film does not need its interior. The relic's removal and its return are stated once, in the chronicle's own terms, and are never dramatised, reconstructed, scored, or framed as a wound or a triumph; no shot is set up to evoke either. No verdict is passed on the king, the kingdom or its ending, and nothing in the film may read as though a capital fell because of what anyone deserved. Where the sources disagree about a date, a height, a step count or an attribution, the film either carries the disagreement or leaves the figure out.
position_hint: late in the group: it is the film that withdraws the reward. It wants the group's films about wanting already seen, so that a flat refusal to call effort a virtue lands as the sources' own position rather than as contrarianism. No location reasoning is involved.
risks: Admiring the workmanship into a moral. The whole film is pointed at the finest carving of its century and the digest's position is that effort has no colour of its own and runs downhill as readily as up [C021-P:L53]; a single reverent sentence in the voice, or one raking-light frame that makes a spectacle of the relief, loses the subject.
'Hard work is always virtuous', which the digest rules out by name. Effort in these sources is morally colourless and can power harm as easily as good.
'Follow your passion', also ruled out by name: the same wish inside a greed-rooted mind strengthens the greed, so drive on its own guarantees nothing [C021-P:L75].

Putting a thirteenth-century king, his ministers or his masons into C006's catalogue. Everything that book classifies is a greed-rooted mind, the group's hazard is precisely that a camera cannot show greed, and beats 6 and 7 exist to name the catalogue and then decline to apply it to anybody.

Kamma as fate. A capital that lasted about a decade, a relic carried off, a dynasty in decline: the material invites a reading in which the ending was deserved, and the floor forbids it outright. No beat, no frame and no cut may imply a verdict on the king or on the kingdom's collapse.

Reading rapture, resolve or conviction onto a carved face or a living one. The sources' account of gladness shaking and lifting the body through the air element is traditional physiology [C021-P:L61], and the decision factor is described as settling firmly whether it is right or wrong [C021-P:L45]; neither is a description of anybody on camera or in granite.

Repeating IDEA-0003. That film is the same archetype — rock citadel, grand stairway, abandoned height — and shares a country, a century of scholarship and a shape. This film must carry no argument from a missing sculpture, no visitors' inscriptions, no ascent, no dawn or dusk or night, no summit and no view, and no aircraft; and its voice never mentions the lions at all, although they are the site's most famous objects and one of them is on a banknote.

Presenting restored stonework as original. At least one popular account states that the stair was badly damaged after the king's death and that what is seen now is a reconstruction; this could not be confirmed and it has to be settled with the Department of Archaeology before a frame of it is used as thirteenth-century carving.
Becoming a heritage documentary about an ephemeral capital. The history is the argument, not the content; the moment the voice starts explaining the site, the film has lost its subject.

Averaging the numbers. The rock's height, the reign dates, the step counts, the date of the relic's return and the dimensions of the pierced windows all differ between sources, and the temptation to give the viewer one clean figure is the temptation to invent one.
The narrowness and steepness of the flight, which is a safety and courtesy problem before it is a production one, and which means some frames may simply not be obtainable without holding people up.
drop_if: The carving cannot be filmed in available light without chalking, wetting or artificial raking light.

The riser panels turn out to be modern re-cut or replacement work, or the extent of restoration cannot be established, since the payoff frame is the film and it has to be honestly what the voice says it is.
Frames on the flight cannot be got without obstructing the only route up.
Permission is offered only on condition that the site is presented as a heritage showcase, or that the relic's removal is narrated as a national injury.

connections.note: The slate's other rock-citadel film, and the reason nearly every choice here is a refusal. That one is an ascent from first light to dusk, built on a name with nothing under it, a wall of visitors' verses, a gateway's surviving paws and a summit. This one is a single duration in flat midday light, on carved granite, on a stair it never climbs as a story, with no missing-sculpture argument, no inscriptions, no dawn, no night, no summit, no view and no aircraft. Its payoff is one riser, not a horizon.

The group's other film on the same concept, and the two halves of one simile filmed apart: here the hand that grips the vessel firmly while the other rubs it slowly, in exterior granite at midday; there an interior floor of imported tiles at a raking angle. Effort that produced a masterpiece, against a find nobody was looking for.

The group's third film on the same concept, and its opposite case. There the labour was compulsory and its purpose was ornament; here the labour is anonymous and its purpose was an approach to a relic. Both refuse a verdict on a king, and both keep the atrocity or the loss to a single flat statement.

selection.reason: It is the group's plainest demonstration that effort is not a virtue, and it is the only location on the slate where the quantity of visible effort is overwhelming and everything that would grade it morally is gone. The location was chosen for the story first: a chronicle that gives a duration in one sentence and a stair that is the whole surviving evidence of it. Legacy merge recommendations were cleared on 2026-09-25 and this field records executed merges only; none has been executed here.

review.note: Rewritten from the ground up and relocated, so any earlier verdict on this record refers to nothing. The old film was a one-day kite festival on a northern beach: an honest working-place film that carried C021 only by resemblance — the place happened to look like the sources' similes — and it also put a camera on a community's own festival day in order to make a philosophical point, which is a cost the film could not pay. It goes. The new location is a thirteenth-century rock citadel in the dry zone whose ornamental stairway is the finest figure carving of its century on the island, and the binding is historical rather than pictorial: the Culavamsa gives the king who ruled from that rock eleven years of government in a single sentence and almost nothing else, the chronicle's own text is defective at the point where it describes the famine that preceded the end, the palace was never on the summit, the relic the stair was built to approach was carried to the mainland and negotiated back into a different city, and what survives of the whole enterprise is a worked surface and a number. That is C021's question standing in the open — is effort a merit? — because everything that could answer it has gone and only the effort is left. C006 is kept as the sorting scheme the site cannot answer, named in two beats and applied to nobody. The guards, in order of how easily they would be broken: the film must not admire the labour into a moral, so the digest's boat-on-a-downstream-current line is spoken over the payoff frame itself; no thirteenth-century person goes into the greed-rooted catalogue, which is the group's hazard; kamma is not fate and the loss of the capital carries no verdict; the relic's capture and return are stated once, flat, in the chronicle's terms, never as wound or triumph; nothing is chalked, wetted, raked or lit, and restored stonework may not be passed off as original; no worship at the living temple at the foot is filmed; and every separation from IDEA-0003 is deliberate — no lion argument, no visitors' inscriptions, no dawn, no night, no ascent, no summit, no view, no aircraft. Research corrected four things the brief's own note carried: the eleven years is the length of the reign in the chronicle and not a dated span of capital, the rock is most often given as 90 m rather than 100 m, the summit was not an unfinished palace because the palace was never there, and the relic's return is dated only by modern reconstruction and did not come back to this rock. Five Commons images verified.

suggested_location.name: Yapahuwa rock citadel and its ornamental stairway

also_known_as.name: Subhagiri, Subhapabbata, Subhacala, Sundarapabbata
also_known_as.meaning: Subha's rock, Subha's mountain, the beautiful mountain; the Pali forms used in the Culavamsa, which Geiger's footnote identifies with 'the present so-called Yapahu'

also_known_as.name: Yapavva / Yapahuva
also_known_as.meaning: the older Sinhala form; the Wikipedia article states the original name was Yapawwa and that the modern form is a distortion of it, and Lankapradeepa reports a form Yapawa in early Brahmi inscriptions
also_known_as.used_by: Sinhala usage and the site's signage

also_known_as.name: Yapahuwa Rajamaha Vihara
also_known_as.meaning: the living temple of Kandyan date at the foot of the rock, with cave images and later paintings

suggested_location.region: Kurunegala District, North Western Province; on the dry-zone plain in the Mahawa (Maho) area, reported as south-east of Maho and roughly midway between Kurunegala and Anuradhapura
suggested_location.elevation_note: Figures for the rock's height above the surrounding plain differ and are kept apart rather than averaged: 90 m (300 ft) is the commonest figure and is what the Wikipedia history section and two other accounts give, while the same article's opening sentence says the rock rises 'abruptly almost a hundred meters above the surrounding lowlands'. One account places the palace terrace at about 35 m above ground level, in a saddle on the southern slope. The summit's height above sea level was not established in this research, and none of these figures was checked against a survey.
suggested_location.why_here: Because the concept's question is asked here by the record rather than by resemblance. C021's hardest claim is that effort is not a merit — it runs like a boat on water already flowing downhill, and the good deed is the same load carried uphill — and this is the one place on the slate where the effort is overwhelming, undeniable and completely detached from anything that would grade it. The ornamental stairway is among the finest medieval Sinhalese stone carving there is: risers of the top flight cut with a female dancer between two male drummers, panel after panel, figures about a hand's width across, with makara balustrades, dwarfs, and the largest surviving lion sculptures of the old kingdoms at the foot. And the entire enterprise it belonged to is summarised by the chronicle in one line about eleven years of government. The stair goes up to a doorway and the outline of a relic house, not to the top; the relic it was built to approach was taken to the mainland and negotiated back into another city; two of the pierced stone windows from its porches are in museums and the openings they sat in are empty. So the site hands the film exactly what the concept needs and nothing it must not have: a colossal quantity of visible, skilled, patient work, a duration, and no evidence whatsoever about the wanting behind it. It also delivers the cinema in the same objects, at a distance of inches, which is why this film needs no aircraft, no crowd, no weather and no golden hour to work.

historical_thread.story:
The rock was a Buddhist monastery for something over a thousand years before it was briefly a royal capital. Lankapradeepa reports large bricks bearing the earliest type of Brahmi letters as masons' marks on the upper part of the rock, and early Brahmi inscriptions of the first century CE recording the donation of a tank to the monks; the Wikipedia account notes a Brahmi inscription in one of the caves at the base, alongside a cave shrine with Buddha images, and a ruined stupa called Kota Wehera, a bodhi-tree enclosure and a small pond on the summit. A living temple of Kandyan date, the Yapahuwa Rajamaha Vihara, stands at the foot with cave paintings of that period.

The fortress on the rock was not the work of the king the site is famous for. Modern accounts agree that it was raised by a Sinhala general named Subha as a stronghold against the Kalinga invader Magha, who held Polonnaruwa in the first half of the thirteenth century, and the Pali names for the place — Subhagiri, Subhapabbata, Subhacala, Sundarapabbata — carry his name; Geiger's footnote to the Culavamsa states flatly that Subhacala and its synonyms are 'the name for the present so-called Yapahu'. The chronicle then puts the building of the royal town there in the previous reign to the famous one. At Culavamsa 88.77-79, Vijayabahu IV, having fought and beaten Candabhanu's Javaka army in that country, 'had this town (Subhagiri) also surrounded by a high rampart and a trench and built there a superb royal palace. Having finished it, he established then in that town a regular almsgiving for the great bhikkhu community. Then he spake encouragingly to his younger brother King Bhuvanekabahu and made him take up his abode as before in Subhapabbata.' The younger brother was living on the rock before he was king, and the rampart, the trench and a royal palace are credited to the elder.

Vijayabahu IV was killed by his own Senapati, Mitta. Chapter 90 opens with Bhuvanekabahu escaping the rebel: he springs from his litter, reaches a village, takes a good elephant from a stall where elephants were tethered, recrosses a river in flood, and 'the King reached that selfsame Subhagiri'. Mitta seated himself on the lion throne in the old capital and was beheaded there by the Ariya warrior Thakuraka, whose men told the assembled Sinhala soldiers that 'it took place at the command of King Bhuvanekabahu who abides in Subhagiri'. The warriors then brought him down from the rock to the old capital and consecrated him king. He drove back the Damila forces and the Vanni kings, 'took up his abode for several years' in the old capital, and only then 'betook himself thereupon to the town of Subhagiri, had built here an extensive royal city, gleaming in the beauty, and abode there'. The chronicle credits him with having the whole Tipitaka copied out and distributed, with repeated ordination festivals, and with celebrating 'daily a great sacrifice for the Tooth Relic'. Then the single sentence that gives this film its number: 'In this wise he wrought good, while dwelling in Subhagiri and after carrying on the government for 11 years, he entered heaven.' The eleven years is a reign, not a dated span on the rock, and the same chapter has him spending several of those years at the older capital first.

The Tooth Relic's presence on the rock is an inference rather than a statement. Geiger's own footnote says that according to Culavamsa 89.41 Vijayabahu had deposited the Tooth and Bowl Relics at Polonnaruwa, and that 'evidently his successor had brought them back to Subhagiri to the town built by him there, a theory supported by 90.41' — the verse about the daily relic sacrifice. Modern accounts state as fact that Bhuvanekabahu I brought the relic with him from Dambadeniya and enshrined it in a temple built for it at the head of the third staircase.

The end is four verses long. 'Once when (here in Lanka) a famine arose there landed, sent with an army by the five brothers, the kings who held sway in the Pandu realm, a Damila general known by the name of Ariyacakkavattin who though he was no Ariya was yet a great dignitary of great power. He laid waste the kingdom in every direction and entered the proud stronghold, the town of Subhagiri. The sacred Tooth Relic and all the costly treasures there he seized and returned with them to the Pandu kingdom. There he made over the Tooth Relic to King Kulasekhara.' Geiger notes that the text is defective exactly here: 'There is a gap in the text here. Of v. 43 a the MSS. have only chatasmim, five syllables are therefore wanting.' He also notes that Kulasekhara reigned 1268-1308 on Codrington's chronology, and that Ariya Cakravartin is named in a South Indian inscription reported in the Annual Report of Epigraphy, Southern Circle, Madras Government, 1903.

The recovery is negotiation and nothing else. Parakkamabahu III 'reflected: "That Tooth Relic which was taken to the Pandu kingdom - that relic of the Prince of the wise, our highest protecting deity, worthy of veneration by our race, how shall I bring it back from there?" And as the Ruler saw no other means but friendly negotiation, he set forth in the company of several able warriors, betook himself to the Pandu kingdom and sought out the Ruler of the Pandus. By daily conversations he inclined him favourably, received from the hands of the King the Tooth Relic, returned to the Island of Lanka and placed the relic in superb Pulatthinagara in the former relic temple.' The relic did not come back to the rock. The rock, in the Wikipedia account, was 'largely abandoned and inhabited by Buddhist monks and religious ascetics' - which is to say it went back to being what it had been before.

What is left of the eleven years is the stone. Three flights of stair climb the southern flank; accounts of their step counts differ and are set out below. The top flight is the celebrated one: its risers and balustrades carry the figure carving, most panels showing one female dancer between two male drummers, with makaras at the balustrade ends, crouching dwarfs, elephants and lions, and at the foot the two lion sculptures described as the largest surviving from the old kingdoms - the left-facing seated lion on the front of the Rs 10 note of the Central Bank's 1991 Sri Lanka Heritage series, whose catalogue description reads 'Yapahuwa Stone sculpture of seated Lion facing left with head down mouth open on right'. Several writers note that these lions, with their goggled eyes and wild manes, resemble Chinese lion sculpture, and that more than a thousand Chinese coins and fragments of celadon and porcelain have been recovered in and around the site, which puts a thirteenth-century maritime trade relationship behind the observation without settling anything about the carving. The porches above the stair held pierced stone windows cut through with rings of small figures; one is in the national museum in the capital and one in the museum on site, and the openings they came out of are empty. H. C. P. Bell, the first Archaeological Commissioner, worked here from the 1890s and is credited with unearthing the staircases and with finding the Chinese material and the mason's-marked bricks. And the palace was never on the summit. One account places it on a terrace in a saddle on the southern slope; the summit carries the ruined stupa, the bodhi-tree enclosure and the pond, which belong to the monastery rather than to the city.
historical_thread.how_it_binds:
C021's most uncomfortable claim is that effort has no moral colour of its own. The Pradeepika's picture for it is exact and unflattering: in a person whose mind is already inclined towards harm, effort behaves like a boat set on water that is already flowing downhill, arriving easily and needing nothing; and the good deed is a load carried uphill, where the effort has to be deliberately put in. The digest draws the conclusion in one line - effort is not a virtue in itself, and where it goes depends on the slope it is placed on. A film has to find somewhere that makes this visible rather than arguable, and a great deal of undisputed effort with the slope removed is exactly what this site is.

Start with the quantity. The top flight of that stair is the best figure carving anyone in this country produced in that century. It is granite. The figures are inches high. They repeat along the flight and no two of them do the same thing. Whoever cut them held the work with one hand and went over it slowly with the other, which is the Pradeepika's own picture for sustained application, not a resemblance to it. Nothing about the labour is in doubt and nothing about it is small.

Now remove the slope. The chronicle gives the whole enterprise one sentence - eleven years of government, and then he entered heaven - and the sentence is about a reign, part of which was spent somewhere else. The building of the rampart and the palace belongs to the elder brother. The relic's arrival is Geiger's inference from a verse about a daily offering. The verse that describes the famine at the end is defective in every manuscript. The relic was taken and then handed back after daily conversations and placed in a different city. Two pierced stone windows came out of the porches and are in museums; their openings are empty. The palace was never on the summit, so there is not even the tidy story of an unfinished crown. What survives, in other words, is the effort and the duration, and not one of the things that would tell you what the effort was for in anybody's mind. That is the concept's own position handed over as a site condition: the stone tells you that somebody pushed, and it cannot tell you which way the ground was tilted.

C006 is the reason the film can say that without hedging. The sources do have an apparatus for grading wanting, and it is precise: glad or flat, with a story or without, risen on its own or pushed - and, against expectation, flat outranks glad and unpushed outranks pushed. Point that apparatus at a carved riser and every dial reads nothing. You cannot recover from granite whether the order was given gladly or coldly, whether it came with a justification, or whether the man who gave it had to talk himself into it. A film that guessed would be inventing a greed-rooted mind for a thirteenth-century person, which is the one thing this group must never do; a film that names the apparatus and then reports that the site answers none of it is doing what the sources do, which is to describe a mechanism and then decline to apply it where the evidence is absent.

The last thing the history supplies is the guard the film needs most. A capital of about a decade, a famine, an invasion, a relic carried off, a rock that reverts to being a monastery: this is an almost irresistible invitation to a verdict, and the floor forbids it. Kamma is not fate and no ending is deserved. The chronicle helps here, because its own account of the recovery is neither a battle nor a humiliation - a king went in person, talked daily, and was handed the relic - and because the sentence about the famine is broken. The film states the sequence once, in the chronicle's terms, and spends the rest of its length on a step.
what_is_certain: Yapahuwa is a rock citadel in Kurunegala District, North Western Province, on the dry-zone plain in the Mahawa (Maho) area, and it is a ticketed archaeological site with a museum on it.

The Culavamsa in Geiger's translation identifies Subhacala, Subhagiri, Subhapabbata and Sundarapabbata as names of the place, with the translator's footnote calling them 'the name for the present so-called Yapahu'.

Culavamsa 88.77-79 states that Vijayabahu IV 'had this town (Subhagiri) also surrounded by a high rampart and a trench and built there a superb royal palace', established a regular almsgiving in it, and made his younger brother Bhuvanekabahu 'take up his abode as before in Subhapabbata'.

Culavamsa chapter 90 opens with Bhuvanekabahu escaping the rebel Senapati Mitta and reaching Subhagiri; the Ariya warrior Thakuraka then killed Mitta, stating that it was done 'at the command of King Bhuvanekabahu who abides in Subhagiri', after which the army brought him from Subhagiri to Jambuddoni and consecrated him king.

The same chapter states that he took up his abode 'for several years' at Jambuddoni and only afterwards went to Subhagiri and 'had built here an extensive royal city, gleaming in the beauty, and abode there'; that he had the whole Tipitaka copied and distributed; and that he 'celebrated daily a great sacrifice for the Tooth Relic'.

Culavamsa 90.42 reads, in Geiger's translation: 'In this wise he wrought good, while dwelling in Subhagiri and after carrying on the government for 11 years, he entered heaven.' The eleven years is the length of the reign as the chronicle gives it.

Culavamsa 90.43-47 records a famine, an army sent by 'the five brothers, the kings who held sway in the Pandu realm' under a general 'known by the name of Ariyacakkavattin', his entry into 'the proud stronghold, the town of Subhagiri', his seizure of 'the sacred Tooth Relic and all the costly treasures there', and his handing of the relic to King Kulasekhara.
Geiger's footnote to 90.43 records a defect in the text: 'There is a gap in the text here. Of v. 43 a the MSS. have only chatasmim, five syllables are therefore wanting.'

Geiger's footnotes state that Kulasekhara reigned 1268-1308 on H. W. Codrington's chronology, and that Ariya Cakravartin is mentioned in a South Indian inscription (No. 110 in the Annual Report of Epigraphy, Southern Circle, Madras Government, 1903, per Codrington).

Culavamsa 90.51-55 records that Parakkamabahu III 'saw no other means but friendly negotiation', went to the Pandu kingdom himself with several able warriors, 'by daily conversations he inclined him favourably, received from the hands of the King the Tooth Relic', and 'placed the relic in superb Pulatthinagara in the former relic temple'. The chronicle records no military threat and the relic was not returned to Yapahuwa.

Geiger's footnote states that according to Culavamsa 89.41 Vijayabahu had deposited the Tooth and Bowl Relics at Pulatthinagara, and that 'evidently his successor had brought them back to Subhagiri to the town built by him there, a theory supported by 90.41'. The relic's presence on the rock is therefore the translator's inference from the chronicle rather than a statement in it.
The Wikipedia account states that after the relic's capture the site 'was largely abandoned and inhabited by Buddhist monks and religious ascetics'.
The ornamental stairway rises in three flights on the southern flank, and the Tooth Relic temple stood at the head of the third flight, not on the summit.

The summit carries a ruined stupa called Kota Wehera, a bodhi-tree enclosure and a small pond; there are caves at the base, one with a shrine and Buddha images and one with a Brahmi inscription; a temple of Kandyan date, Yapahuwa Rajamaha Vihara, stands at the foot with paintings of that period.

Lankapradeepa reports large bricks with the earliest type of Brahmi letters used as masons' marks on the upper part of the rock, and early Brahmi inscriptions of the first century CE recording the donation of a tank to the monks, so the site was a monastery long before it was a capital.

There is a fortification at the southern base with ramparts and moats. Lankapradeepa gives a semicircular plan with three ramparts, a moat and three causeways, an inner rampart of about 200 m diameter and an outer of about 450 m, and outer ramparts exceeding 800 m in length at an average height of about 7 m.
The carving of the top flight includes makara balustrade ends, dwarfs, elephants, lions and panels of dancers and musicians, with most panels reported as one female dancer between two male drummers.

The two lion sculptures at the foot of the balustrades are described as the largest surviving lion sculptures of ancient Sri Lanka, and the seated lion appears on the front of the Central Bank's Rs 10 note of the 1991 Sri Lanka Heritage series; the banknote catalogue at notes.lakdiva.org.lk describes the design as 'Yapahuwa Stone sculpture of seated Lion facing left with head down mouth open on right'.
Pierced stone windows from the porches above the stairway survive: one is in the national museum in the capital and one in the museum on the site.

H. C. P. Bell, the first Archaeological Commissioner of Ceylon, worked at the site from the 1890s and is credited with unearthing the staircases; Chinese coins in quantity, celadon and porcelain fragments, and the mason's-marked bricks are attributed to that work and to later excavation.
what_is_disputed: The height of the rock above the plain. 90 m (300 ft) is the commonest figure and is given by three of the accounts read; the Wikipedia opening sentence instead says 'abruptly almost a hundred meters above the surrounding lowlands'. The brief's own note gave about 100 m. The figures are kept apart and none is preferred.

The reign dates and the dates of the capital. 1272-1284 (Wikipedia lead and CCF), 1273-1284 for the capital with the palace and fortress 'built by King Buvanekabahu I (1272-1284) in the year 1273' (Wikipedia history section), 1273-1284 for the reign (AmazingLanka), 1272-1284 (Lankapradeepa), and 1271-83 (Lanka Excursions) all appear. The Culavamsa gives no year at all, only eleven years of government.

What the eleven years counts. The chronicle's eleven years is the length of Bhuvanekabahu I's reign, and the same chapter has him living 'several years' at the older capital before moving to the rock, so the period during which the rock was the capital is shorter than eleven years and is not dated by any source read here. Modern accounts treat 1273-1284 and 'about eleven years as the capital' as interchangeable, and they are not.

Who built what. Culavamsa 88.77-79 credits Vijayabahu IV with the high rampart, the trench and 'a superb royal palace' at Subhagiri, and has Bhuvanekabahu living there before his accession; 90.30 credits Bhuvanekabahu with building 'an extensive royal city' there. Modern accounts almost uniformly state that Bhuvanekabahu I built the palace and fortress in 1273, which the chronicle does not support without qualification. Modern accounts also credit the original stronghold to General Subha against Kalinga Magha, which is not established from the chronicle text read here.

Whether the summit was unfinished. Nothing found supports it. The accounts read state that the palace was not on the summit at all but on an intermediate terrace, one of them placing that terrace in a saddle on the southern slope at about 35 m above ground level, and the summit carries monastic remains - a ruined stupa, a bodhi-tree enclosure and a pond. The brief's note that 'the summit was never completed' is not the finding; that the palace was never there is.

The step counts. 'Around 100 steps' at 'an abrupt 70-degree angle' (Wikipedia lead of the architecture section); a three-flight breakdown of about 15-20, then a 'speculative' 30-40, then 40-45 (the same article, lower down); a middle section of 65 steps and a final flight of 35 (Lanka Excursions); and 'the final ascent of 35 ornate steps' (AmazingLanka and others). The 70-degree figure appears without a source anywhere it appears.

The date of the relic's return. 1288 is given by Wikipedia and by Lanka Excursions and is repeated everywhere; the chronicle gives no date, and Parakkamabahu III's reign is given as 1287-1293. The year is a modern reconstruction and is reported as such.

How the relic was recovered. The chronicle says negotiation and only negotiation - the king 'saw no other means but friendly negotiation'. The Wikipedia architecture section adds 'and threats in regards of military attacks', for which nothing was found, and which the chronicle's own wording contradicts.

The pierced stone window's dimensions and the date it was found. 'A slab 1.4 metres (4 feet 7 inches) thick with 45 pierced circles', found in 'an 1850 excavation', is repeated verbatim across several pages including AmazingLanka. A pierced window slab 1.4 m thick is not credible and the figure most likely belongs to a height or a width in the source it was copied from; the 1850 date also sits awkwardly beside the attribution of the staircase's excavation to Bell in the 1890s. Neither figure is used as fact. The comparison of the window to the tracery of the Taj Mahal appears in the same block of copied text and is not treated as a scholarly judgement.

Whether the stairway as it stands is original or restored. One tourism account states that the staircase 'was badly damaged during the Pandyan invasions following the king's death, and what is seen now is a reconstruction'. No conservation report was found either way. This matters more than anything else on this list, because the film's payoff frame is one riser presented as thirteenth-century carving, and it has to be settled with the Department of Archaeology before shooting.

The Chinese question. Several writers observe that the Yapahuwa lions, with goggled eyes and wild manes, resemble Chinese lion sculpture, and note over a thousand Chinese coins and celadon and porcelain fragments from the site as evidence of a direct thirteenth-century trade relationship. That the trade material was found is reported consistently; that the carving was influenced by Chinese models is offered as a possibility by the writers themselves and is recorded here as an open question, not as a finding. A claim that the Chinese traveller Wang Dayuan visited and described the fortress in the fourteenth century appeared in one search summary and was not found in any page read.

The 'fire rock' etymology, which appears in the title of one older blog post and in scattered travel writing, has no support in anything read here. The name's derivation is given by Lankapradeepa as possibly from a form Yapawa in early Brahmi inscriptions, and by Wikipedia as a distortion of an original Yapawwa; neither is presented as settled.

Above all, nothing in this record grades anybody. The chronicle's account of the invasion, the famine and the relic is a sequence of events recorded in a partisan source whose text is defective at the crucial verse, and it is not evidence about the moral state of any king, general, minister, mason or community. The film records the layers and adjudicates none of them, and no part of this history may be read as a verdict on why a capital ended.

what_to_film: The whole rock from the level of the plain at midday, in one locked frame from far enough back that the ramparts are in the foreground and the stair is a pale line on the flank. This is the opening and the closing frame and it needs no aircraft.
The ornamental flight square-on from directly in front on a long lens, far enough back that the perspective flattens and the stair reads as a worked surface at an angle rather than as a climb.

One riser of the top flight, level, square and locked off: a female dancer between two male drummers, each figure about a hand's width. This is the payoff and everything else is arranged around getting it clean, in available light, with nothing applied to the stone.
Three or four further riser panels at the same distance and the same light, so that the repetition and the variation between them are both visible without a single camera move.
A makara balustrade end whole, then a macro frame of bare granite beside it: tool marks, pits, lichen, and the difference between cut stone and rock.
A balustrade lion in one wide static frame only, for reference and for the record's sake. The voice never mentions it and it carries no beat.
The porch opening above the stair from below and level, empty, with plain sky behind it, and then the same opening long so that the emptiness fills the frame.

The threshold stone at the head of the flight, straight down from standing height, worn smooth in two places; and the outline of the relic house platform beyond it, wide and static, filmed from the threshold without going through.
Heat shimmer at the base of the rock in the dry months, long lens, as the film's only moving element.
suggested_location.access: A ticketed archaeological site under the Department of Archaeology, with a museum on site, reached by road in the Mahawa area and signposted from the Kurunegala-Anuradhapura road; no walk-in of any length is required to reach the foot of the stair. The ornamental stairway is steep and narrow - narrow enough in places that visitors go up sideways - and is the only route to the doorway and the relic-house platform, so it is the whole site's bottleneck. Professional filming needs permission from the Department of Archaeology, and the extent of past restoration of the stairway has to be established with them before any frame of the carving is used. The film is deliberately built to need no aircraft, so a drone refusal costs it nothing. There is a living temple with a shrine and paintings at the foot; it is not needed and is not entered. Visitor numbers are low on ordinary days compared with the better-known citadels. Monkeys are present; snakes are a dry-season consideration on the rock.
suggested_location.best_time: The dry months, and within the day the middle of it - roughly ten to two, with the sun high and the south-facing flight lit flat and frontally, which is the light this film requires and the light most films avoid. A flat overcast is equally usable and arguably better. Low raking light is specifically not wanted, since it dramatises the relief and makes a spectacle of the labour. No dawn, no dusk, no night.

suggested_location.research_note: All of this is desk research by web search on 26 September 2026 and none of it has been checked on the ground or against a printed edition. The Culavamsa material is the exception in quality and is the spine of the record: Geiger's translation was downloaded as the Internet Archive full text of volume 2 and read directly at the passages quoted, so chapters 88 and 90 and the translator's footnotes are quoted from the text itself rather than from a summary, and the eleven-year sentence, the rampart-and-palace attribution to Vijayabahu IV, the manuscript gap at the famine verse and the negotiation-only recovery were all read in place. Everything else comes from the secondary pages listed. The Wikipedia article was read in full as plain text through the API. The CCF page, AmazingLanka, Lankapradeepa, Lanka Excursions and the lakdiva banknote catalogue were fetched and read through a summarising fetch rather than in raw form, so their wording is reported at one remove and the phrasings attributed to them should be re-checked before any of them is quoted in a film. Two pages reached this research only through search-result summaries and were not fetched: ceylonhistory.com and the Daily FT article on the site; nothing in the record rests on either, and the '35 ornate steps', '45 pierced circles' and '1.4 metres thick' figures that circulate in that block of text are recorded in what_is_disputed as unverified and in one case not credible. Coordinates are the Wikipedia point for the site (7.816784, 80.310746) and are not a surveyed position on the stairway. The Department of Archaeology's museums page was located but not read. The three things a pre-visit has to settle are, in order: how much of the ornamental stairway is original and how much is re-set or restored, since the payoff frame depends on it; whether the riser panels read in flat available light from a tripod at step height; and whether frames can be got on a narrow single-file flight without holding anyone up. No permission has been sought. No image of a single carved riser panel, and none of either pierced stone window, exists on Wikimedia Commons as far as this search found; the five images listed were each confirmed by title through the Commons query API before their URLs were written, and the two staircase files are the closest available to the film's central subject.

unknowns: The extent of past restoration of the ornamental stairway is unknown and is the single most important open question, because the film's payoff frame presents one riser as thirteenth-century carving.
No filming permission has been sought from the Department of Archaeology, and the conditions attached to filming the carving at close range are unknown.
Whether the riser panels read at a hand's width in flat available light, from a tripod at the height of the step, has not been tested.
Whether frames can be obtained on a steep single-file flight without obstructing visitors, and whether an early or low-season window exists, is unestablished.

The rock's height, the reign dates, the step counts, the date of the relic's return and the dimensions of the pierced windows all differ between sources and none has been resolved against a survey, an inscription or a scholarly edition.

Nothing is known about how the site's custodians, or the community at the living temple at the foot, would want the relic's removal and return described, and that is theirs to decide rather than the film's.
evidence_class_note: Editorial proposal. The location is Claude's suggestion and awaits Chathura's verdict. The Culavamsa passages are quoted from Geiger's published translation as digitised by the Internet Archive; everything else is desk research from the secondary sources listed, with the disagreements between them recorded rather than resolved, and none of it is documentary evidence. No scene or shot is decided here; the sequence is a shape for the film, not a shot list.
